This completes the lesson on Brushless DC (BLDC) Motor Controllers.

One of the largest BLDC motor/controller combinations is used to position huge radio telescopes. The motor runs on 600 VDC or higher voltage and the controllers are often water-cooled. The transistor switches are high power Field Effect Transistors (FETs)...
The controller is usually part of a user interface chip. The motor is sensor less and the load is an off-balanced weight.
One of the smallest BLDC motor/controller combinations is familiar to most people. The vibrator in a pager, wristwatch, personal data assistant (PDA), and cellular telephone is a BLDC.

Precise speed control is provided by a crystal-controlled oscillator. The IC also offers motor shutdown for over-current conditions and a low speed alarm. The IC is a 24-pin surface mount device about the size of a dime...

The illustration is a 3-phase full-wave controller on a single IC. External components are minimal, consisting of the Hall-effect sensors, direction switch, motor drive transistors, crystal input, and an alarm output...

This system of 4-phase BLDC with H-E control is very common in computer and robotics. The pancake motor used in most computer cooling fans is an example of this technology. This method of construction is known as System Integration as all associated circuitry and motor components are integrated into one assembly.....

The H-E IC outputs are complementary; when pin 2 is high, pin 3 is low. You will note power is applied to the coils at all times and the switching is done by forward biasing the transistors, selectively grounding one end of the coils in the desired order...

For simplicity's sake, the H-E ICs are shown in 2 places; realize that each one is a single chip mounted inside the BLDC casing on the stator. The H-E units (HE and HE ) are physically located in the stator. This system uses only 2 sensors and 4 transistor switches.
Let us examine a full-wave bidirectional 4-phase motor system using H-E (Hall-effect) sensors for manual circuit switching. The sensors are labeled HE and HE on the schematic diagram.

The full-wave motor controller requires three photodiode or Hall effect sensors, six output transistors, and a logic control unit. The sensors are used as inputs to the logic unit, which turns the output transistors on and off...
The system works perfectly in theory, of course, but what ensures that the rotor is moving as directed? This is where the sensors come into play.

There are many of the possible switching combinations but only six are needed to control the full-wave motor in either direction of spin. Two coils are always active to ensure rotational direction is maintained...

Notice each pair of transistor switches is complementary, Q through Q are PNP, and Q through Q are NPN. This allows each winding location, A, B, and C, to be driven with a positive or a negative voltage, reversing the magnetic field in the associated winding of the full wave motor..e motor..
The full-wave motor controller allows motor action in both directions. This type of motor is ideal for continuous duty applications requiring motor reversal.

The three-phase configuration in our example is a unipolar BLDC motor. It provides clockwise rotation to serve any number of purposes quite fully. However, rewiring of the motor or its circuits would be required to deliver both clockwise and counterclockwise motor action...

When the rotor is aligned with winding , the shutter cutout exposes photodiode Q . A voltage is sent to transistor Q , and S is energized, pulling the rotor clockwise to end in its original position.....

Without light to , transistor is turned off. The light that reaches causes it to generate a voltage, which turns on transistor and energizes winding . The magnetic forces move the rotor further clockwise....

When S is energized, a south magnetic field is produced at the pole face, and the north pole of the rotor is attracted. The rotor revolves in a clockwise direction to align itself with S . The shutter cutout moves, blocking Q and exposing Q .
The light through the shutter cutout causes Q to generate a voltage, which turns on transistor Q . Q amplifies the current to energize the stator winding S .

When the north pole of the rotor is aligned with the stator winding S , light reaches photodiode Q through the opening in the shutter. Notice that the other transistors are off, as the shutter blocks light from Q and Q .

intervals. The three photodiodes, Q , Q , and Q , are connected through driver circuitry to Q , Q , and Q , which switch power to S , S , or S dependant upon the position of the rotating shutter.
Regardless of the number of wires, the operation BLDC motor is the same. Typical construction uses either a three-phase or a four-phase format. Let's look at the three-phase configuration first...

In this eight-wire BLDC motor system, three wires provide power to the three-stator windings. The other five wires are for three sensors. Two of the five wires are used to power the sensors and the remaining three are used for the sensor outputs...
In contrast to the two-wire motor, the commutation electronics of a multiple-wire BLDC motor may be mounted externally or located in a separate enclosure.
Additional features are also available for the two-wire BLDC motor, such as a third wire for feedback capability and an on-board potentiometer for speed control.
Although two-wire BLDC motors are usually limited in size to approximately 1/3 horsepower, hybrid commutation electronics have been developed for higher horsepower requirements.

The major advantage of the two-wire motor is the simple connection: one wire for the power supply and one wire for the power return. However, since the commutation electronics are enclosed within the motor case, heat generation is a concern with this type...

Another factor of BLDC design involves the number of connections and the location of the commutation electronics (CE). Compare the Two-Wire BLDC type and the Multiple-Wire BLDC type. Two-Wire BLDC Multiple-Wire BLDC

Why are Hall-effect sensors preferred to photodiodes in the BLDC motor system?
Photodiodes are too large for BLDC applications.
Hall-effect sensors are more accurate than photodiode sensors.
Hall-effect sensors sense the position of the BLDC rotor without additional mechanical hardware or electronics.

Hall-effect sensors provide a voltage output when there is a magnetic field of proper polarity (north or south) with sufficient current to drive a load. The voltage is sent to the commutation electronics (driver) circuit to properly power the stator windings...

The placement of the device is critical so the field generated by the stator windings does not trigger the Hall-effect sensor. Hall-effect (H-E) sensors are placed between the rotor and stator to sense the magnetic position of the rotor...

The Hall-effect sensor detects magnetic fields in the immediate area. Unipolar H-E sensors only have one sensor incorporated into the IC. There are other more intricate types of H-E sensors.
The H-E circuit is a simple pulse generator consisting of a voltage regulator, hall voltage generator (magnetic sensor), amplifier, Schmitt trigger, and (2) output transistors.
The LED/photodiode (optical) sensor is gradually being replaced by Hall-effect technology for increased reliability and reduced costs. Fewer components are used in the Hall-effect sensor system...

Because the current from the photodiode cannot generate a magnetic field strong enough to cause motor action, a power transistor is connected. The stator windings are energized, and the correct rotation is achieved...

At a precise moment, the position of the cutout in the shutter allows the light from the LED to reach the photodiode. The photodiode generates a voltage for the length of time the light strikes it, until the shaft rotates the cutout away and the solid shutter breaks the path...

The LEDs are placed strategically on the BLDC motor, and a photodiode for each is placed exactly opposite. The shutter, which is attached to the motor shaft, rotates between the pair. The cutout portion of the shutter allows the light from only one of the LED's to reach its corresponding photodiode at a time...

The optical type of sensor, the LED/photodiode pair, consists of a light source (LED), a rotating disk (also known as a shutter), and a photodiode. The diodes convert light into data pulse. light into data pulse....

Both optical and magnetic sensors are used to detect the rotor's position in a BLDC motor. The two most popular types of sensors are the LED/photodiode pair (optic) or the Hall-effect device (magnetic)...
The BLDC motor uses sensors to determine the rotor position and speed. These sensors then generate signals that control the switching of the windings (commutation electronics).

Of course, optimum BLDC construction is to use no more sensors and power semiconductors than necessary. Increasing the number of electronic elements increases the cost of the motor. Unnecessary electronic devices dramatically increase the cost without improving functionality...

The current capability of the rotor position sensor circuits is limited. Therefore, power semiconductors are used to increase the small current output from the sensor circuits to the amount of current needed for the stator windings...

As you can see, precision timing is necessary to keep the rotor moving smoothly. Rotor position sensor circuits track the rotor position and switch the power to the windings. As in any motor system, it takes a specific amount of current to generate a magnetic field strong enough to cause motor action...

The second major difference between the two motors has to do with the shaft position sensor. The conventional DC motor uses a tachometer to indicate motor speed..
BLDC motors reverse the DC motor operation: the magnet moves, not the windings.

The main difference between the two motors involves the positioning of the magnetic field that changes to control the rotation. Conventional DC motors vary the field in the armature (rotor) with the stator in a fixed position...

However, with optimum construction, the long-term cost for a BLDC motor is frequently less than that for a conventional DC motor, even if the initial investment is larger.

BLDC has not replaced many conventional PM type motors. An automobile starter, an application usually best suited to conventional DC motors, is an example of here-to-stay technology. Starter motors work for a long time in adverse environments, and they are relatively inexpensive...

An integrated assembly application that is used on millions of PCs all over the world is the muffin fan on the motherboard. Fans are the most common use of this application.

Medical and dental applications require special casings because the motors must be sterilized. In other words, the motor must be sealed. This requirement is perfect for BLDC applications because the motors may operate without cooling air...

Commercial applications are used for kitchen appliances, automobile luxury features, powerboats, consumer entertainment products, and remote control hobbyists. These motors are lower cost because the application is much less stringent or demanding...
High power applications start at about 500 pound-inches of torque and beyond. High power motors drive hoists, conveyor belts, and pumps.
More phases are associated with less power but higher precision.

The Two Phase and Three Phase motor applications are commonly used with 360 degree rotation requirements. High performance Three Phase motors are widely used and provide the smoothest acceleration for the cost...

The One Phase motor, also called a Limited Angle Torque or LAT, only rotates a fraction of one full rotation. Scanners, cameras, precision gimbal systems, value controllers, transmissions, and aircraft use this motor application...
High performance BLDC motors are further characterized by the phase of the motor (number of stator windings). These are: One Phase Two Phase Three Phase
If the load is rigorous, demanding a high torque to inertia ratio and a duty cycle near 100%, a high performance motor is the solution.

High performance BLDC motor requirements may be satisfied by either industrial or miniature types. A pancake motor operating at 100,000 RPM is an example of a miniature high performance application...
BLDC applications may be listed in 6 categories: High performance High power Commercial Medical and Dental Integrated Assembly Custom Design

Miniature BLDC motors are widely used, in everything from remote control devices to computers. The hard drive in your computer has a high-speed BLDC motor driving it. Another term for miniature is pancake...
BLDC motors are found in two general types: Industrial and Miniature. Industrial motors are large and have high torque and power ratings.

High torque and angular acceleration, along with the capability for continuous operation as well as low maintenance requirements, make this type of motor optimum for applications such as gyroscopes, CD ROM drives, and computer hard drives...

The relationship of angular acceleration (a), torque ( T ), and rotational inertia ( I ) can be expressed mathematically by a formula.
The difference in momentum and inertia caused by the lower mass of the BLDC rotor allows the motor to reach operating speed faster and respond to changes in speed more quickly.
The list of advantages of BLDC over conventional motors continues. Without windings attached to the rotor of a BLDC motor, the weight and mass of the rotor is reduced.
Reduced friction allows increased acceleration, contributing as well to the other advantages of durability, cooler operation, and noiselessness.

Further advantages are derived from reduced friction. The brushes of DC series motors rub on the commutator to produce friction. In the BLDC motor, however, the only frictional forces are those that arise from the bearings. Conventional DC Motoral DC Motorrr

No matter how small the generated spark might be, the end result is interference that could disrupt the operation of electronic equipment in close proximity to the motor. This hazard is avoided by BLDC technology...

Radio frequency interference (RFI) is caused by the sparks that are produced when brushes contact the rotating commutator. At each instant that current begins to flow from the brush to the conductor segment, a spark is generated.....

In DC series motors, audible noise is produced when the brushes contact the conductor segments and the insulation surfaces of the commutator. The noise tends to increase as these surfaces exhibit wear at different rates. mmutator Segments Segment/Insulation Wear Conventional DC Motorrrrr
There are two different kinds of noise avoided by BLDC motors: audible noise and radio frequency interference.

Not only are BLDC motors cooler and more durable than conventional motors, they are also quieter. Operation of these motors is relatively noise-free, as the interference caused by brushes contacting and sparking on the commutator is completely avoided...
These factors of BLDC construction allow the motor to keep cool so that it can operate in a continuous mode for long periods of time.
In the BLDC motor, the permanent-magnet rotor does not generate heat. The current in the stator windings produces heat that is easily dissipated through the case.
In a conventional DC motor, heat generated in the rotor tends to build up until it is transferred to the stator, through the stator, and then to the cooler ambient air.
Conventional DC Motor Brushless DC Motor

Besides eliminating excess heat from arcing, the BLDC construction facilitates rapid dissipation in another way. The stator is mounted on the surface of the case instead of being enclosed like the DC series motor. Conventional DC Motor Brushless DC Motorrr

Without voltage leakage, there is no arcing between the commutator contacts and the brushes. Thus, excess heat is not generated to add to the dissipation demanded by the normal operation of current through the electromagnetic windings...
BLDC motors are maintained at the stator, not the rotor. It is not normally necessary to pull a rotor on a BLDC motor.

Anyone who has disassembled a conventional DC motor understands the reduced maintenance advantage of the BLDC. The brushes produce black soot that seems to stick to everything it shouldn't, and the technician ends up looking like a coal miner...

How does brushless make the difference? It's quite simple. There are no brushes to cause wear on a commutator or to wear out themselves. Parts that do not wear out do not produce conductive dust that must be removed to prevent voltage leakage paths...

Characteristics of BLDC produce advantages over the DC series motors you've studied previously. Brushless translates into cleaner operation and lower maintenance, as well as increased reliability and longer life...

What determines the phase of a BLDC motor?
The manufacturer's design revision level, which determines the position of the windings on the outside surface of the case.
The particular application, which determines where the motor is used in the sequence of program operation.
The number of windings, which determines the amount of control and therefore the smoothness of the rotation.

The casing protects the other subsystems from radio frequency interference (RFI), heat, light, moisture, or other unwanted external influence. The case bears the markings that identify the motor type, rating, manufacturing data, and other pertinent information. ----

The rotor position sensors are used, as the name implies, to determine the position of the rotor in relation to the stator. Position information enables specific stator windings to be energized and meet the exact direction and speed of shaft rotation required...

The third basic component of a BLDC motor involves the commutation electronics. Electronic switches power and rotate the magnetic field around the stator according to signals received from the sensors...

Notice that the electrical components of the BLDC are located in the stator, where they are not only more accessible for examination and repair but they are also stationary. The conventional motor rotates the electrical components...

The stator windings, which provide the rotational direction from the control system, are situated on the outside surface of the case. The number of windings, or phase, of the BLDC motor is a critical design characteristic. The more windings, the more control, and therefore, the smoother the rotation...

The BLDC rotor is a permanent magnet, and, unlike its conventional counterpart, it is not slotted. In a kind of design reversal, the BLDC rotor appears more like the stator of a conventional DC motor...
The BLDC motor consists of four basic components: Rotor Stator Commutation electronics (electronic switches and drivers) Rotor position sensors

Why are BLDC motors characteristically smaller than their conventional permanent magnet DC motor counterparts?
The BLDC lacks brushes and bulky commutator components.
The conventional motor has higher load ratings in all instances.
The BLDC is used in applications that require smaller dimensions.

Naturally, without the brushes, the internal space required is reduced. Therefore, BLDC may be seen as smaller overall. While this may often be the case, the characteristic of size is driven by the applications of BLDC, not by the design of the mechanical system...

BLDC doesn't use brushes for commutation. Externally, the difference between a brushless DC motor and a conventional one may be difficult to ascertain, as the primary BLDC characteristics are internal to the motor case...

BLDC technology has both macro and micro applications; it is essential to high power servomotors as well as miniature drive mechanisms. The electronics are the same in everything from a heat-shielded module to a microchip, just scaled down or up depending on the purpose to be served...

Electronic control over mechanical functions has changed many fields. Industrial controls, aviation technology, marine engineering, weapons, communications - the list goes on and on. The backbone of this engineering science is the rotating machine (motor), and a particularly useful type is the brushless DC motor (BLDC).....
